1. Antenatal hydronephrosis (ANH)

  • Definition of hydronephrosis? Antenatal?
  • Hydronephrosis = dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces (the collecting system). It describes anatomy, not cause — a dilated system is not necessarily obstructed. ANH = hydronephrosis first detected on prenatal (fetal) ultrasound.
  • Rule of thumb: dilated ≠ obstructed. Many ANH cases are physiologic or transient — the postnatal work-up exists to find the kidneys that are actually at risk (obstruction, reflux, bladder outlet obstruction).
Added explanationCommonly used thresholds: renal pelvis AP diameter ≥ 4 mm at 16–27 weeks or ≥ 7 mm at ≥ 28 weeks; ≥ 10 mm postnatally.

Postnatal evaluation — history

  • Maternal health: maternal PMHx & FmHx — GU anomalies, course of pregnancy, DM, meds · previous pregnancies: siblings with VUR, hydro · gender of the child · voiding (1st void, straining, wetting the diaper) · EtOH, drug use.
Ask aboutWhy it matters
Maternal healthDiabetes and teratogenic drugs raise anomaly risk; family GU disease suggests a heritable cause
Previous pregnanciesVUR is familial — positive family history in ~30%
GenderPUV only occurs in boys — changes the bilateral differential completely
VoidingDelayed first void, straining or a poor stream point to bladder outlet obstruction (PUV)

Pre-natal US

  • Gender of fetus · single vs multiple · AF volume · kidneys: degree of hydro, variation between exams, unilateral/bilateral · ureters: hydroureter · bladder: presence, fullness, size, thickness, emptying · urethra: dilated posterior urethra · other abnormalities · overall growth and development.
  • Oligohydramnios → bilateral obstruction or poor renal function → risk of pulmonary hypoplasia. Unilateral → UPJO most likely; bilateral → PUV (boy) or VUR. A dilated ureter puts the problem at or below the UVJ (UVJ obstruction, VUR, PUV) — not the UPJ. Big, thick-walled bladder that doesn't empty → outlet obstruction (PUV). Dilated posterior urethra — "keyhole" → PUV.

Oligohydramnios

  • Oligohydramnios = amniotic fluid < 500 cc (pocket < 2 cm). Before 16–18 wks most AF is a placental transudate; by 20–22 wks most AF is fetal urine; urine production starts at ~12 wks.
  • Oligohydramnios that develops only after 18–20 weeks likely represents GU tract obstruction or abnormal renal development.
  • Clinical link: low AF in mid-gestation restricts fetal lung growth → pulmonary hypoplasia — why a baby with PUV may need NICU respiratory support before anything urological is done.

Investigations

  • US · VCUG · nuclear scan. No IVP.
TestWhat it showsUse it to…
Ultrasound (renal & bladder)Degree of hydronephrosis, parenchyma, ureters, bladder size and wall; no radiationConfirm ANH after birth; follow it; first test in every case
VCUGContrast instilled into the bladder by catheter, films while filling and voidingDiagnose and grade VUR; show a dilated posterior urethra in PUV
Nuclear scan (diuretic renogram)Tracer uptake (split renal function) and drainage after Lasix (T½)Tell an obstructed kidney (UPJO) from a dilated but draining one
Added explanationNo IVP in neonatal hydronephrosis — newborn kidneys concentrate contrast poorly (poor images), plus radiation and a contrast load.

Normal renal & bladder US — kidney with a compact central echo complex; full, thin-walled bladder

Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) — preliminary film, bladder filled with contrast, voiding phase showing a normal-calibre urethra

  • How to read it: pre-Lasix — both kidneys take up tracer (split function); Lasix (~20–27 min) → diuresis washes tracer out. T½ = time for half the tracer to leave the kidney after Lasix. Short T½ = drains well; a curve that stays flat = obstruction.
Added explanationT½ < 10 min = normal drainage · 10–20 min = indeterminate · > 20 min = obstructed. Split function < 40% in the affected kidney is significant.

Post-natal work-up

  • Serum Cr. (when and why?) · prophylactic antibiotic · repeat US ± VCUG or nuclear scan.
  • Serum creatinine: baseline renal function (essential in bilateral hydro, PUV, solitary kidney). Draw it after ~48 h — in the first days it reflects the mother's creatinine.
  • Prophylactic antibiotic: protects a dilated, possibly refluxing or obstructed system from UTI while the work-up is pending.
  • Repeat US ± VCUG or nuclear scan: US confirms and grades; VCUG if reflux or PUV is suspected; nuclear scan if obstruction is suspected.
Added explanationThe routine first postnatal US is usually done after 48 h (neonatal oliguria can hide dilatation) — earlier if bilateral hydro or PUV is suspected.

Differential diagnosis of ANH

UnilateralBilateral
UPJ obstruction 39–64%Posterior urethral valves 2–9%
UVJ obstruction 9–14%Vesicoureteral reflux
Vesicoureteral reflux 33%Urethral aplasia
MCDK 4–25%Prune belly syndrome
Ureterocele / ectopic ureter · duplex systemMegacystis–megaureter
PCKD · physiologic · extra-renal pelvisPCKD

UPJO · PUV with bilateral hydroureteronephrosis · VUR during micturition · ureterocele

  • Rules of thumb: unilateral → UPJO is the single most common cause. Bilateral in a boy → exclude PUV first (the dangerous one). Bilateral in a girl → PUV is off the list; think VUR. VUR appears in both columns.
  • Most common cause of antenatal hydronephrosis → pelviureteric junction obstruction. 439

2. Case 1 — bilateral hydronephrosis in a boy: posterior urethral valves

  • Case 1: 2-day-old term boy (SVD), bilateral hydronephrosis on antenatal US. What are the possible causes? How would you manage this case?
Case 1 slide — the differential to recall (answers masked) (1)

Postnatal US — hydronephrotic kidneys with dilated calyces and a distended bladder

Fetal US — distended bladder funnelling into a dilated posterior urethra ("keyhole" sign)

VCUG — large irregular bladder above a dilated posterior urethra; reflux into a dilated, tortuous ureter and collecting system

  • Posterior urethral valve (PUV): congenital obstructive membrane in the posterior urethra that impedes antegrade flow of urine.

Cystoscopy — the obstructing valve membrane in the posterior urethra

  • Back-pressure dilates everything above it: posterior urethra → bladder (thick, trabeculated) → ureters → kidneys.
  • High-risk pattern: boy + bilateral hydroureteronephrosis + distended thick-walled bladder + dilated posterior urethra (± oligohydramnios) = PUV until proven otherwise. Threats to life: pulmonary hypoplasia and renal insufficiency.
  • Newborn boy, bilateral ANH, thick bladder and dilated posterior urethra → best study micturating cystourethrogram (VCUG). 437 ×3
  • Regarding PUV → the child may have a poor stream. 426

Initial management

  • 1) 1st step: bladder drainage (permits medical stabilization). 2) Effective NICU support for pulmonary hypoplasia & renal insufficiency. 3) Labs: electrolytes, creatinine, BUN — may take 48 h to be accurate. 4) Prophylactic Abx. 5) Cystoscopy and valve ablation (definitive treatment).
  • Remember the order: drain first, ablate later. The catheter buys time to stabilize lungs, fluids and electrolytes and to get a true creatinine before definitive valve ablation (once the baby is stable).
  • 3-day-old boy with bilateral ANH → next step insertion of a Foley catheter (bladder drainage). 437 ×2
  • Newborn boy, bilateral hydronephrosis, bladder wall hypertrophy, catheter already inserted → best treatment PUV ablation. 437

3. Case 2 — unilateral hydronephrosis: UPJ obstruction

  • Case 2: 5-day-old boy with unilateral hydronephrosis on antenatal US. What are the possible causes? How would you approach this case?
Case 2 slide — the differential to recall (answers masked) (1)

US — RT kidney: marked hydronephrosis; LT kidney: normal; bladder normal

FeatureNo obstruction (lecture example)RT UPJ obstruction (Case 2)
Curve after LasixFalls steeplyFlat plateau / keeps rising
T½R = 6 min, L = 2 minR = N/A (never reaches half)
MeaningDilated but draining → observeObstructed → surgical candidate

Ureteropelvic junction obstruction

  • Most common cause of UNILATERAL hydro in the fetal kidney · M > F · L > R.
  • Hydronephrosis without hydroureter — the ureter below the narrowing is normal calibre.
  • Work-up: no need for urgent intervention unless the baby develops pyelonephritis → nephrostomy tube or stent · repeat US · treatment is surgical.
  • Pyeloplasty: open / laparoscopic / robotic.
  • Danger point: pyelonephritis in an obstructed kidney needs drainage (nephrostomy or stent) — the one situation in UPJO where you intervene urgently.
Added explanationWhen to operate: split function < 40% or a fall of > 10% · worsening dilatation on serial US · obstructed drainage on renal scan · symptoms (pain, pyelonephritis, stones).
  • PUJO — when to operate → decline in kidney function on MAG3 (renal scan). 439

4. Case 3 — bilateral hydronephrosis in a girl: vesicoureteral reflux

  • Case 3: 5-day-old girl, bilateral hydronephrosis on antenatal US. Possible causes? Approach?
Case 3 slide — the differential to recall (answers masked) (1)
  • First thought: she is a girl, so PUV is excluded — remaining bilateral causes: VUR, urethral aplasia, prune belly, megacystis–megaureter, PCKD. VUR leads the list.

US — bilateral hydronephrosis (LT and RT kidneys) and dilated distal ureters behind the bladder

Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR)

International grading of VUR, grades I–V

GradeContrast reaches…
IA non-dilated ureter only
IIPelvis and calyces, without dilation
IIIMild–moderate dilation of ureter, pelvis and calyces; minimal blunting of the fornices
IVModerate ureteral tortuosity and dilation of pelvis and calyces
VGross dilation of ureter, pelvis and calyces; loss of papillary impressions; ureteral tortuosity
  • Presentation: ANH (30–40% due to VUR) · UTIs · family Hx (30%).
  • Work-up: US · VCUG.
  • Treatment options: observation · prophylactic antibiotics · surgical: Deflux injection · ureteric reimplantation.

Ureteric reimplantation (ureter re-tunnelled submucosally) and Deflux (bulking agent coapts the refluxing orifice)

  • Principles of management: 1. Spontaneous resolution is very common. 2. High-grade VUR is less likely to resolve spontaneously. 3. Extended use of prophylactic Abx is benign. 4. Success rate with surgical correction is very high.
  • Deflux = endoscopic bulking agent injected under the ureteric orifice so it closes during bladder filling. Reimplantation = open re-tunnelling of the ureter under the bladder mucosa to make an anti-reflux valve.
  • 1-year-old girl, recurrent febrile UTIs, normal US, VCUG shows VUR → initial treatment prophylactic antibiotics. 437 ×3

5. Hypospadias

  • 3 anomalies of the penis: 1. abnormal ventral opening of the urethral meatus · 2. ventral curvature · 3. a dorsal "hood" and deficient ventral foreskin.

Hypospadias — dorsal hooded foreskin with ventral meatus; proximal meatus (arrow)

  • Distal (glanular · subcoronal · distal penile) — the majority. Mid — midshaft. Proximal (proximal penile · penoscrotal · scrotal · perineal) — more curvature, more complex repair.
  • Epidemiology: ~1 in 250 live male births · the majority are distal · can be familial · more in twins.
  • Diagnosis: most found at newborn P/E · some diagnosed later or after circumcision · no routine imaging for isolated hypospadias.
  • Physical exam: abdominal exam · external genitalia · micropenis · meatal location · hernia · hydrocele · UDT.

Be aware

  • Do not circumcise — the foreskin is tissue for the repair; a baby with hypospadias should not be circumcised before the urologist sees him.
Added explanationCheck the testes: hypospadias with undescended testes (especially proximal hypospadias or impalpable testes) raises concern for a disorder of sex development → evaluation (e.g. karyotype).
  • 3-month-old with hypospadias brought for circumcision → don't circumcise — re-evaluate later. 437 ×3 (Peds page)

Reasons for repair & surgery

  • 1) Micturition in standing position · 2) sexual intercourse · 3) effective insemination · 4) cosmesis — distal hypospadias → cosmesis.
  • Surgical repair at 6–12 months of age, in 1 or 2 stages.
Added explanationOne stage usually suits distal cases with mild curvature; staged repair suits proximal cases with severe curvature.

6. Exstrophy–epispadias complex

  • 3 main variants: 1. epispadias · 2. bladder exstrophy — > 50% of kids born with this complex · 3. cloacal exstrophy — much more GI involvement.
  • Epispadias: males > females · requires surgical repair after the age of 1 year · some patients will have issues with incontinence.

Epispadias — dorsal meatus in a boy; in a girl the arrow marks the urethral opening

FeatureHypospadiasEpispadias
MeatusVentral (underside)Dorsal (top side)
How commonCommon — ~1 in 250 boysRare; part of the exstrophy–epispadias complex
ContinenceNormalMay be impaired
Repair timing6–12 months, 1 or 2 stagesAfter 1 year

7. Prune belly syndrome

  • Triad: 1. weak/absent abdominal muscles · 2. bilateral UDT · 3. weak and dilated GU organs (bladder, ureters, urethra). Other: tetralogy of Fallot · VSD.

Prune belly syndrome — protuberant abdomen in an older boy; lax, wrinkled abdominal wall in a newborn

  • A bilateral cause of ANH from weak, dilated muscle — not from a blockage. Examine the heart.
Added explanationPrune belly vs PUV (both bilateral ANH in a boy): PUV = anatomical obstruction, normal abdominal wall, testes usually descended, first step bladder drainage. Prune belly = functional (weak smooth muscle), lax wrinkled wall, bilateral UDT, supportive care + cardiac evaluation.
